1.why: Each 255 is 8 network bits, so three of them make 24. The last octet 224 is 11100000, adding 3 more bits for a total of /27.

2.why: A /26 leaves 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, which gives 64 addresses. You lose the network and broadcast addresses, so 62 are usable. 64 is the tempting trap.

3.tip: 5 host bits means 3 network bits left in the last octet: 128+64+32 = 224.
3.why: The last octet has 8 bits. If 5 are for hosts, the other 3 are network bits (11100000), which is 224 in decimal, so the mask is 255.255.255.224.

4.why: Going from /24 to /26 borrows 2 bits from the host part. 2 bits can make 4 combinations (00, 01, 10, 11), so you get 4 equal subnets of 64 addresses.

5.tip: 4 subnets = borrow 2 bits = /26 = .192 mask. Block size 64: .0, .64, .128, .192. Second one is .64.
5.why: Four subnets need 2 borrowed bits, so the mask is /26 (255.255.255.192). Each subnet is 64 addresses wide, so they start at .0, .64, .128 and .192. The second is .64.

6.tip: 2 bits = 4 networks (too few). 3 bits = 8 networks (enough for 5).
6.why: Each borrowed bit doubles the subnet count. Two bits give only 4 subnets, which is not enough for 5. Three bits give 8, so you must borrow three.

7.tip: /26 always gives 62 hosts, no matter where the subnet starts.
7.why: A /26 has 6 host bits, so 2^6 = 64 addresses. Take away the network and broadcast addresses and 62 are left for hosts. The starting address .128 doesn't change the count.

8.tip: 252 in the 3rd octet = /22, so 10 host bits: 1024 - 2 = 1022.
8.why: 255.255.252.0 is a /22, which leaves 10 host bits. 2^10 = 1024 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses, gives 1022 usable hosts.

9.tip: Private trio: 10 /8, 172.16 /12, 192.168 /16. The prefix grows as the first number grows.
9.why: RFC 1918 sets aside these three ranges for private use inside homes and companies. 169.254 is link-local, 100.64 is shared carrier space and 239 is multicast.

10.tip: /22 = blocks of 4 in the 3rd octet. 16 to 19, so broadcast is .19.255.
10.why: A /22 covers 4 values in the third octet, so 172.16.16.0/22 runs from 16.0 to 19.255. The broadcast address is the last one: 172.16.19.255.

11.why: You need 7 host bits because 2^7 - 2 = 126. That leaves 25 network bits, which is 255.255.255.128. The .224 and .240 masks hold only 30 and 14 hosts.

12.tip: 25 hosts need a /27 (30 hosts). The exhibit uses .0-.63 and .192-.207, so .64/27 is free.
12.why: A /27 gives 30 hosts, enough for 25. The exhibit already uses 10.16.10.0/26 (.0 to .63) and .192/28, so .64/27 (.64 to .95) is free and doesn't overlap.

13.cue: usable number of host IP addresses on a network that has a /26
13.why: A /26 leaves 6 host bits, 2^6 = 64 addresses. The first is the network address and the last is the broadcast, so 62 can be given to hosts.

14.tip: Multicast = Class D = 224 to 239. 240 and up is experimental.
14.why: IPv4 multicast addresses are the Class D range, 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255. 240 and above is reserved, 169.254 is link-local and 127 is loopback.

15.tip: 192.168.x.x is private: it can't be reached across the Internet without NAT or a VPN.
15.why: 192.168.25.10 is in a private RFC 1918 range. Private addresses are not routed on the Internet, so school A can't reach it directly without a VPN or NAT.

16.tip: Cross out the private ones: 10.x, 172.16-31.x and 192.168.x. What's left is public.
16.why: Public addresses are ones outside the private ranges. 192.168.1.245, 10.15.250.5 and 172.31.1.25 are private, so the other three are the public ones.

17.cue: all hosts on a remote network
17.tip: Directed = aimed at a REMOTE network. Limited = 255.255.255.255, stays local.
17.why: A directed broadcast is sent to the broadcast address of another network, like 172.16.4.255, so it can be routed there. A limited broadcast never leaves the local network.

18.tip: 18 hosts need /27 (30). 10 hosts need /28 (14). Both must sit inside .64 to .127.
18.why: The space is 192.168.1.64/26, which runs from .64 to .127. .64/27 (.64 to .95) holds 30 hosts for the 18, and .96/28 (.96 to .111) holds 14 hosts for the 10.

19.tip: Link-local starts with FE80. Think 'FE80 = Free Every-link 80'.
19.why: IPv6 link-local addresses come from FE80::/10, so they start with FE80 to FEBF. FD80 and FC90 are unique local, FEC8 is old site-local and FE0A is outside the range.

20.tip: Rule 1: drop leading zeros. Rule 2: :: only ONCE.
20.why: You can drop leading zeros (00AB to AB, 0057 to 57) and replace one run of zero groups with ::. Using :: twice is illegal, so the other zero pair stays as 0:0.

21.cue: subnets can the administrator create from the /48
21.why: The interface ID is the last 64 bits, so you can only subnet between /48 and /64. That is 16 bits, and 2^16 gives 65,536 subnets.

22.cue: last subnet that is created if the subnet prefix is changed to /52
22.tip: /48 to /52 = 4 bits = the FIRST hex digit of the 4th group. Last value: f, so f000.
22.why: Going from /48 to /52 uses 4 bits, which is the first hex digit of the fourth group. Those subnets count 0000, 1000, up to f000, so the last one is 2001:db8:0:f000::/52.

23.cue: type of IPv6 address is FE80::1
23.tip: FE80 = link-local. ::1 alone would be loopback.
23.why: Any IPv6 address starting with FE80 is link-local, used to talk only on the local link. The ::1 at the end is just the interface part, not the loopback address ::1.

24.cue: maximum number of subnets achieved per sub-site
24.why: In the exhibit the subnet section is a single hex digit. One hex digit is 4 bits, which can hold 16 values (0 to F), so each sub-site can have 16 subnets.

25.tip: EUI-64 = 48-bit MAC + FFFE in the middle = 64-bit interface ID.
25.why: EUI-64 takes the 48-bit MAC address of the interface, splits it in half, puts FFFE in the middle and flips the 7th bit. That makes a 64-bit interface ID.

26.tip: /64 = the first 4 groups (each group is 16 bits).
26.why: Each IPv6 group is 16 bits, so a /64 prefix is the first four groups: 2001:DB8:BC15:A. Everything after that (12AB::1) is the interface ID.

27.tip: FF02::1 = ALL nodes. FF02::2 = all routers.
27.why: FF02::1 is the all-nodes multicast address. Every IPv6 device on the local link listens to it, a bit like a broadcast in IPv4. FF02::2 would reach only routers.

28.cue: communication between devices on the same link
28.tip: Link = FE80. FC00::/7 is unique local, 2001 is global.
28.why: FE80::/10 is the link-local range. These addresses only work on the local link and routers never forward them. FC00::/7 is unique local and 2001 is global unicast.

29.cue: unicast address that is assigned to multiple hosts
29.tip: ANYcast: the same address on many hosts, ANY nearest one answers.
29.why: An anycast address is a normal unicast address given to several devices. Packets go to the nearest one, which is how many DNS servers share one address.

30.cue: two types of IPv6 unicast addresses
30.tip: Unicast = one to one. Loopback (::1) and link-local (FE80) each point to one interface.
30.why: Unicast addresses identify one interface. Loopback ::1 and link-local FE80 addresses are both unicast. Multicast and anycast are their own types, and IPv6 has no broadcast.

31.cue: without using a server that keeps a record
31.tip: SLAAC = Stateless Address AutoConfig: the device builds its own address, no server keeps track.
31.why: With SLAAC the router sends its prefix in a Router Advertisement and the device makes its own global address. No server tracks addresses, unlike stateful DHCPv6.

32.tip: SLAAC rides on ICMPv6 Router Solicitation and Router Advertisement messages.
32.why: SLAAC uses ICMPv6 messages: the host sends a Router Solicitation and the router answers with a Router Advertisement holding the prefix. DHCPv6 is a different method.

33.tip: 127.0.0.1 = loopback = talking to yourself. It tests your own TCP/IP stack.
33.why: 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address. The ping never leaves the computer, so it only checks that TCP/IP is installed and working on that host, not any cable or network.

34.tip: Look at the last hop that answered (192.168.1.254 = R1). Trouble starts just after it.
34.why: The first hop, 192.168.1.254, is R1's gateway address, and then every hop times out. So packets reach R1 but go no further. Start troubleshooting at R1.

35.cue: traceroute command to send and receive echo
35.tip: Echo request and echo reply are ICMP messages, the same ones ping uses.
35.why: Echo requests and replies, plus the time exceeded messages traceroute relies on, are all ICMP messages. ICMP reports how IP packets are doing.

36.cue: hop limit field of a packet is decremented to zero
36.tip: Time ran out = TIME EXCEEDED. Hop limit (IPv6) is the same idea as TTL (IPv4).
36.why: Each router lowers the hop limit by 1. When it hits zero the router drops the packet and sends back an ICMPv6 time exceeded message. Traceroute uses this to find each hop.

37.tip: Hop limit counts DOWN. At zero, the packet is dropped.
37.why: Every router lowers the Hop Limit by one. When it reaches zero the router drops the packet and sends time exceeded back. It counts down, so it never climbs to 255.

38.tip: ICMP is IP's feedback channel: it reports problems but does not fix them.
38.why: IP doesn't guarantee delivery, so ICMP sends feedback, like destination unreachable or time exceeded, to tell the sender what happened to a packet. It doesn't ensure delivery.

39.cue: source IP address does a router use by default
39.tip: The packet leaves through an interface, so it wears that interface's address.
39.why: By default a router uses the address of the interface the packet goes out of as the source. It doesn't pick the highest, lowest or loopback address unless you tell it to.

40.tip: IPv4 unreachable codes: 0 Net, 1 Host, 2 Protocol, 3 Port. 'No Hungry People Present'.
40.why: In ICMPv4 destination unreachable, code 1 means host unreachable: the network was reached but the host could not be. Code 0 is network, 2 protocol and 3 port.

41.tip: /26 from .64 runs .64 to .127, and .96 sits in the middle.
41.why: 192.168.1.64/26 covers .64 to .127, with .65 to .126 usable, so .96 fits. The /27, /28 and /29 choices end before .96 (at .63, .47 and .71).

42.tip: Remember the pattern: ::1 on subnets 1 and 2, then ::2 on subnet 3.
42.why: In the Packet Tracer activity you check the IPv6 addresses actually configured on the devices. These three are the ones the activity finds; the others are not set on any device.

keys.k: all hosts in the same subnet

43.tip: Broadcast = everyone in MY subnet. Routers stop it at the edge.
43.why: A broadcast goes to every host in the local subnet. Routers don't forward broadcasts, so it never goes out to the whole Internet.

44.why: A unicast is sent from one host to one specific destination host. Multicast goes to a group and broadcast goes to everyone in the subnet.

45.tip: ICMPv6 codes: 0 no route, 1 prohibited, 2 beyond scope, 3 ADDRESS unreachable, 4 port.
45.why: In ICMPv6 destination unreachable messages, code 3 means address unreachable: the router could not reach the destination address. Host unreachable is an IPv4 term.

46.tip: MULTIcast = a group that signed up. Broadcast = all, unicast = one.
46.why: A multicast goes to a group of hosts that joined that multicast group, like devices running the same routing protocol. Only group members process it.

47.tip: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and swap ONE run of all-zero groups for ::.
47.why: Remove leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0008 to 8, 0001 to 1) and replace the three 0000 groups with :: to get 2001:db8::a0b0:8:1.

48.tip: Use :: for the LONGEST run of zeros. A single 0000 becomes just 0.
48.why: Drop leading zeros (09ea to 9ea, 0fe0 to fe0, 0290 to 290). The lone 0000 becomes 0, and the two zero groups in a row become ::.

49.tip: Only LEADING zeros go. Trailing zeros (c400) stay.
49.why: Drop leading zeros (0042 to 42, 0010 to 10, 0909 to 909), keep c400 as it is, and replace the three 0000 groups with ::.

50.tip: Two zero runs? Use :: for the longer one, write the other as 0.
50.why: The two 0000 groups after db8 become ::. The later single 0000 becomes 0. Leading zeros drop (0ab8 to ab8, 0001 to 1), but 1000 keeps its zeros.

51.tip: One zero group can still be written as ::. Leading zeros drop, trailing ones stay.
51.why: Drop leading zeros in each group (0420 to 420, 00c4 to c4, 0025 to 25, 0190 to 190, 0990 to 990) and replace the single 0000 group with ::.

52.tip: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and swap ONE run of all-zero groups for ::.
52.why: Remove leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0008 to 8, 0001 to 1) and replace the three 0000 groups with :: to get 2001:db8::a0b0:8:1.

53.tip: Three zero groups after fe80 collapse to ::. Then trim leading zeros.
53.why: The three 0000 groups become ::, and leading zeros drop (0220 to 220, 0b3f to b3f, 0029 to 29), giving fe80::220:b3f:f0e0:29.

54.tip: Two rules: drop leading zeros in each group, and swap ONE run of all-zero groups for ::.
54.why: Remove leading zeros (0db8 to db8, 0008 to 8, 0001 to 1) and replace the three 0000 groups with :: to get 2001:db8::a0b0:8:1.

55.tip: Only LEADING zeros go. Trailing zeros (c400) stay.
55.why: Drop leading zeros (0042 to 42, 0010 to 10, 0909 to 909), keep c400 as it is, and replace the three 0000 groups with ::.

56.tip: Use :: for the LONGEST run of zeros. A single 0000 becomes just 0.
56.why: Drop leading zeros (09ea to 9ea, 0fe0 to fe0, 0290 to 290). The lone 0000 becomes 0, and the two zero groups in a row become ::.

57.cue: receives a response that includes a code of 2
57.tip: ICMPv6 code 2 = beyond scope: like using a link-local source to reach a far network.
57.why: In ICMPv6, code 2 means beyond scope of the source address. For example, a link-local source address can't be used to reach a destination on another network.

58.tip: IPv4 unreachable codes: 0 Net, 1 Host, 2 Protocol, 3 Port. 'No Hungry People Present'.
58.why: In ICMPv4 destination unreachable, code 1 means host unreachable: the network was reached but the host could not be. Code 0 is network, 2 protocol and 3 port.

59.tip: ICMPv6 code 3 = ADDRESS unreachable. Count: 0 route, 1 prohibited, 2 scope, 3 address.
59.why: For ICMPv6 destination unreachable, code 3 means the address could not be reached. Code 0 is no route, 1 is administratively prohibited and 2 is beyond scope.

60.tip: IPv4 code 0 = Network unreachable. 'No Hungry People Present': 0 Net, 1 Host, 2 Protocol, 3 Port.
60.why: In ICMPv4 destination unreachable, code 0 means network unreachable: a router has no route to the destination's network.

61.tip: ICMPv6 code 4 = port unreachable, the last one on the list (0 to 4).
61.why: In ICMPv6, code 4 means port unreachable: the packet reached the host, but no application was listening on that port.

62.tip: IPv4 code 0 = Network unreachable. Zero network = no route.
62.why: ICMPv4 destination unreachable code 0 means network unreachable: a router along the path has no route to the network of 198.133.219.8.

63.tip: ICMPv6: 0 no route, 1 prohibited, 2 scope, 3 address, 4 PORT.
63.why: ICMPv6 code 4 is port unreachable: the host got the packet but nothing was listening on the destination port. Note IPv6 numbers differ from IPv4, where port is 3.

64.cue: receives a response that includes a code of 2
64.tip: ICMPv6 code 2 = beyond scope: like using a link-local source to reach a far network.
64.why: In ICMPv6, code 2 means beyond scope of the source address. For example, a link-local source address can't be used to reach a destination on another network.

65.cue: Match the subnetwork to a host address
65.why: A /27 is 32 addresses wide. .32/27 holds .48, .64/27 holds .68, and .96/27 holds .121. .63 is the broadcast of the first subnet and .128 is outside all three.

66.cue: Match each IPv4 address to the appropriate address category
66.tip: Network = first in the block, broadcast = last, anything in between = host.
66.why: Find the block size from the prefix. 10.10.10.128/25 and 172.110.12.64/28 start a block (network). 192.168.1.191/26 and 10.0.0.159/27 end one (broadcast). The others are hosts.

67.cue: satisfy the usable host addressing requirements
67.tip: Biggest network gets the biggest block: 100 = /25, 50 = /26, 25 = /27, 2 = /30.
67.why: Pick the smallest block that fits: A needs 100 hosts (/25 gives 126), B needs 50 (/26 gives 62), C needs 25 (/27 gives 30) and the D link needs 2 (/30 gives 2).

68.cue: Match the IPv6 address with the IPv6 address type
68.tip: ::1 loopback. FF02::1 all nodes. FF02::1:FF.. solicited node. 2001:DB8 global.
68.why: FF means multicast: FF02::1 reaches all nodes, and FF02::1:FF plus the last 24 bits is solicited-node. ::1 is loopback, and 2001:DB8 is a global unicast address.

69.cue: allow IPv6 and IPv4 to co-exist
69.tip: Dual = both run side by side. Tunnel = IPv6 inside IPv4. Translate = convert one to the other.
69.why: Dual-stack runs IPv4 and IPv6 together on the same devices. Tunneling wraps an IPv6 packet in an IPv4 packet. Translation (NAT64) converts between them. DHCP isn't one.

70.cue: Match each description with an appropriate IP address
70.why: Each special range has a job: 127.x is loopback, 169.254.x is link-local, 172.16 to 172.31 is private, 192.0.2.x is TEST-NET for examples, and 240 and up is experimental.
